newsitem.title: FRANCE: 17 die in latest Algerian violence - report.
newsitem.headline: 17 die in latest Algerian violence - report.

text.p: Algerian security forces killed 12 Moslem guerrillas in Algiers after a nearly eight-hour gunbattle around a villa being used as a hideout, an Algerian newspaper reported on Sunday.

And Moslem guerrillas struck again in the southern Algerian Laghouat province killing four people, including two oilworkers, four days after they slaughtered more than 30 passengers in the same area at a fake road block, al Khabar and le Soir d'Algerie newspapers said.
The evening newspaper Le Soir d'Algerie, quoting a union official, said Moslem guerrillas killed two oilmen working for the state-owned oil and gas firm Sonatrach.
"The victims perished in the same circumstances as those killed in a fake road block a day before," said the paper, quoting an official of the 38,000 strong workers' union.
Le Soir said the danger facing workers going to Hassi R'mel gas field might force the authorities to step up efforts to open an airport there to ferry employees by plane from the north.

Moslem guerrillas, aiming to cripple the eonomoy, have killed some oilworkers in the past three years including foreigners. The authorities last year made the southern oil and gas areas "no-go" zones except for those with passes.
Two gunmen, thought to be Moslem rebels, shot dead a homeless man on Saturday at Algiers Place des Martyrs main square, the Algerian newspaper el Watan reported on Sunday.
Security forces, using "heavy means", late on Friday surrounded a villa in the southeastern Algiers' district of el Harrach where 12 rebels took refuge, Le Matin newspaper said.
Al Khabar newspaper said on Sunday that an armed group on Thursday night broke into a Moslem prayer room in Kourdane town in Laghouat province, 340 km (210 miles) south of Algiers.
They killed two people and tortured a third and then damaged the room by setting off a canister gas bomb, al Khabar added.

The prayer room is controlled by Sheikh Ahmed Amar Tidjani, grandson of the widely respected chief of the Tidjani Moslem brotherhood which has thousands of followers in several countries, including Senegal.
An estimated 50,000 people have died in Algeria's violence since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a huge lead.
